claims.text: The sluggish-diffusion paradigm fails at elevated temperatures in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Surface-energy gradients drive Au and Cu segregation to the surface of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Surface segregation creates a rapid atomic-exchange and evaporation pathway that overrides configurational-entropy stabilization.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have an FCC structure.
The initial nanoparticles exhibit elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
At the targeted elevated-temperature regime, surface diffusion coefficients become comparable to bulk diffusion coefficients despite the multicomponent composition.
The dominant segregation and evaporation regime is expected between 600 K and 1000 K.
Nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm have a surface-to-volume ratio greater than 50%.
Segregated Au and Cu form a transient low-energy surface shell.
Configurational entropy can stabilize an FCC high-entropy-alloy phase.
Surface energy in sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt particles provides a thermodynamic driving force for elemental segregation.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt.
Au and Cu surface segregation lowers the activation energy for surface diffusion.
Evaporation of surface-enriched Au and Cu causes particle shrinkage and the progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles.
Surface-energy minimization causes elliptical or icosahedral nanoparticles to become spherical.
Differential elemental evaporation widens the nanoparticle size distribution.
Particles remaining after heating will have Au- and Cu-depleted cores enriched in Co, Ni, and Pt.
A sufficiently large composition shift may produce a phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism is valid only below 10 nm because surface-energy contributions then exceed bulk entropy contributions, whereas bulk thermodynamics dominate above 50 nm.
